AbstractText.Label: INTRODUCTION
AbstractText.content: Lipid metabolism has been suggested to be associated with clinical outcomes of renal cell carcinoma (RCC). In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between preoperative cholesterol level (PCL) and postoperative outcomes of patients with localized RCC.

AbstractText.Label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
AbstractText.content: We retrospectively analyzed the data of 5022 patients surgically treated for nonmetastatic RCC. According to the receiver operating curve of PCL for cancer-specific mortality, we stratified the patients into 2 groups by using a cutoff value of 161 mg/dL. The propensity scores for having low PCL were calculated, and the low PCL group was matched with the high PCL group at a 1:2 ratio. The oncological profiles and postoperative survival of patients were compared.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: A low cholesterol level was significantly associated with adverse pathologic findings, such as higher pathologic stage (P < .001) and large tumor size (P = .002). Furthermore, the low cholesterol group showed significantly worse progression-free, cancer-specific, and overall survival (all P values < .001) compared with the high cholesterol group. Multivariate analysis exhibited a higher PCL as an independent predictor of better progression-free (P < .001), cancer-specific (P = .018), and overall survival (P = .001) after matching. Subgroup analysis according to tumor histology revealed that PCL had a significant relationship with patients' survival in clear cell RCC, but not in non-clear cell RCC.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Decreased PCL was significantly associated with worse pathologic outcomes and also inferior postoperative survival in patients with localized RCC; however, those relationships were significant only in clear cell subtypes.
